Some achievements are measured not by the certificate itself, but by the journey behind it.

Today, I officially received my 𝗠𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 (𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗠𝗲𝗿𝗶𝘁) in 𝗔𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 & 𝗠𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 degree from Liverpool John Moores University. This milestone means far more than adding another qualification—it represents resilience, curiosity, and growth.

𝗧𝗟;𝗗𝗥 👀
✔️ MSc (with Merit) in AI & ML from LJMU
✔️ Hands-on experience building an end-to-end VideoRAG system
✔️ Practical exposure to LLMs, RAG, Multimodal AI, Vector Databases & AI Evaluation
✔️ Stronger foundation for AI Engineering, Enterprise AI & AI Architecture roles

The most defining part of this journey was my dissertation:
"Enriching Visual Question Answering using VideoRAG in the Medical Domain using the MedVidQA Dataset."

It was one of the most ambitious and technically challenging topics I could have chosen within the limited timeline.

The goal was to build an end-to-end AI system capable of understanding complex medical videos, retrieving the most relevant context, generating accurate answers using LLMs, and pinpointing the exact video timestamps.

The journey wasn't easy. From GPU and infrastructure limitations to long experimentation cycles, integrating multiple AI components, and balancing research alongside a full-time job, there were moments when I genuinely questioned whether I'd make it to the finish line.

But every challenge became a lesson.

I learnt that building impactful AI isn't about finding the perfect model—it's about designing reliable systems, making informed trade-offs, embracing failure, and continuously iterating.

This experience gave me practical exposure to VideoRAG, RAG, Multimodal AI, Visual Question Answering, LLMs, Prompt Engineering, Embedding Models, Vector Databases, Semantic Retrieval, and GenAI evaluation frameworks—while fundamentally changing the way I approach problem-solving.

More importantly, it has made me a stronger engineer today and strengthened my foundation for the next phase of my career in AI Engineering, Enterprise AI, and AI Architecture.

A heartfelt thank you to my professors, mentors, peers and friends at upGrad and Liverpool John Moores University, to my family and to everyone who supported me throughout this journey.

Here's to staying curious, taking on daunting challenges, and never stopping learning. Onwards and Upwards. 🚀

text:
When hiring AI talent don't just look for people who can build models, look for people who can solve business problems.
A few recommendations for companies hiring AI professionals:

• Define the business outcome before writing the job description.
• Hire for curiosity and adaptability as much as technical expertise, AI changes too quickly to hire only for today's tools.
• Don't expect one person to be a Data Scientist, ML Engineer, AI Architect, Prompt Engineer, Product Manager and Change Lead.
• Assess real-world problem solving rather than relying on technical interviews alone.
• Prioritise communication skills. The best AI professionals can explain complex concepts to non-technical stakeholders.
• Make sure your data, governance and leadership are ready. AI projects often fail because of organisational issues, not technical ones.
• Be realistic on experience. There are very few people with 10+ years of AI experience because modern generative AI is still new.
• Move quickly. The strongest AI candidates rarely stay on the market for long.

The companies getting the best AI talent aren't necessarily paying the most, they're offering interesting problems, supportive leadership, clear strategy and the opportunity to make a genuine impact.

text:
𝐀𝐈 𝐇𝐢𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐈𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭

One of the biggest mistakes I see companies make when hiring in AI?

They start with the job title.

"𝘞𝘦 𝘯𝘦𝘦𝘥 𝘢𝘯 𝘈𝘐 𝘌𝘯𝘨𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘦𝘳."

The challenge is that 𝐀𝐈 𝐄𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫 has become a broad term.

Two companies can advertise the same title and be looking for completely different skill sets.

One might need someone to integrate LLMs into an existing product.

Another might need someone to build agentic workflows and RAG pipelines.

Another could be looking for an ML Engineer to train and optimise models.

Or a startup may need a Founding AI Engineer to build its AI capability from the ground up.

Same title.

Very different roles.

That's why I think the best AI hiring processes start with a different question:

"𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐦 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐰𝐞 𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐭𝐫𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐯𝐞?"

Once you answer that, the job title, skills and experience become much clearer.

In my experience, the companies that define the problem first attract stronger candidates and make better hires.

🌍 AI Ethics & Bias
The most important post in this entire series.
We have spent 27 days learning how to build AI that works.
Today we talk about building AI that is right.

A model that denies loans to women.
A facial recognition system that misidentifies Black faces.
A hiring algorithm that filters out CVs from certain universities.

None of these were built by evil people.
They were built by well-intentioned engineers who skipped this conversation.
Don't be that engineer. 👇
Where bias enters the ML pipeline
Data
Collection
⚠️ Bias #1
Feature
Engineering
⚠️ Bias #2
Model
Training
⚠️ Bias #3
Evaluation
& Metrics
⚠️ Bias #4
Deployment
& Feedback
⚠️ Bias #5
Bias can enter at every single stage of the ML pipeline — not just in the data.
Fixing bias at deployment is 10× harder than preventing it at data collection.
4 types of bias every ML engineer must know
01
📊 Historical / Data Bias
→ "The data reflects past discrimination — the model learns to repeat it."
If historical data was created in a biased world — the model learns those biases as ground truth. It is not learning what is right. It is learning what was normal — even when what was normal was unjust.
💼 Amazon's hiring AI trained on 10 years of CVs — mostly from men. It learned to penalise CVs that mentioned "women's" (as in women's chess club). Scrapped in 2018.
02
⚖️ Algorithmic / Optimisation Bias
→ "Optimising the wrong objective produces a biased outcome."
A model optimised purely for accuracy on an imbalanced dataset will learn to ignore the minority class. High accuracy — but 0% recall on the group that matters most. The metric was right. The objective was wrong.
🩺 A sepsis prediction model had 90% accuracy — but failed 5× more often for Black patients because training data under-represented them.
03
📏 Measurement Bias
→ "The proxy variable you measure is not the true variable you care about."
Using a proxy that correlates with the target but also correlates with a protected attribute introduces bias through the back door — even when you explicitly exclude sensitive features like race or gender.
🏥 Healthcare algorithm used "healthcare cost" as proxy for "healthcare need" — but Black patients spent less due to systemic barriers, not less need. The model systematically under-served them.
04
🔄 Feedback Loop Bias
→ "The model's predictions change the world — and that changed world becomes the next training data."
Model predicts high crime in area A → police deploy more to area A → more arrests recorded in area A → next model learns area A is high crime. The model's bias self-reinforces with every retraining cycle.
🚔 Predictive policing systems in Chicago and LA showed this exact pattern — amplifying racial disparities with every iteration.

3.Privacy

text:
👥 Tag 14 | Modul 13: Scaling Workforce Potential Skills I + II
👥 Du kannst KI nicht skalieren, ohne die Menschen zu skalieren, die KI betreiben.

An diesem Tag des CAS AI Scaling an der HWZ Hochschule für Wirtschaft Zürich AG geht es um eine der wichtigsten Fragen der KI Skalierung: Wie bauen Unternehmen die Skills, Rollen und Teams auf, die KI langfristig tragen?

Bisher haben wir Strategie, Value Realization, Architektur, Governance, Security, Agentic Systems, AI Product Management, MLOps, Datenökosystem und Responsible AI betrachtet.

Jetzt geht es um die Menschen dahinter.

Im ersten Teil bauen wir die Lernmaschine der Organisation. Die Kohorte entwirft Lernpfade von AI Literacy bis Advanced Tracks, gestaltet Micro Credentials, Bootcamps und virtuelle Labs und entwickelt Assessment Methoden mit Badge Systemen und Lernfortschritts Dashboards.
Dazu kommen Make or Buy Strategien, Kooperationen mit EdTech und Hochschulpartnern, Employer Branding für AI Rollen und gezielte Recruiting Kampagnen.

Mentoring Netzwerke, Guilds und Communities of Practice sorgen für Wissenstransfer und Bindung. Hackathons und klare Karriereleitern schaffen Motivation und Entwicklung.

Die Schweizer Realität aus 2026: 58 Prozent der Unternehmen nennen Fachkräftemangel als Bremse für KI Innovation, und nur 24 Prozent machen KI Schulungen verpflichtend.

Im zweiten Teil geht es um strategisches Talent Management für AI Rollen.
Denn hinter jeder AI Strategie steckt auch eine Skills und Hiring Strategie.
Die Kohorte führt Skill Gap Analysen durch, leitet künftige Bedarfe ab und definiert Job Blueprints für Rollen wie Prompt Designer, ML Engineer, AI Developer, AI Product Owner, AI Architect und AI Ethics Manager.

Wir analysieren den Arbeitsmarkt für AI Talente, Consulting Rates für externe Spezialist:innen und den Lebenszyklus von Teams nach Tuckman: Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing.

Beim Performance Management verbinden wir Vision und OKRs mit individueller Leistung, koppeln diese sauber an AI Model Performance und balancieren Blue Work, also Delivery, und Red Work, also Innovation.
Denn KI Skalierung ist nicht nur eine Technologiefrage. Sie ist eine Workforce Frage.

Dozent:innen für diesen Tag: Mariana Solveig Raschke und Dennis Meier. Sie zeigen euch praxisnah, wie Unternehmen Skills, Rollen, Lernpfade und Talent Management so aufbauen, dass KI nicht an fehlenden Fähigkeiten scheitert.
